I think the issue is that most of the arguments occur over various levels of attainment, ie how well integrated the non-dual is in each person, and most of the dissent has been based on who's more correct, rather than integrating all the different perspectives into a more fully realized transcendent paradigm.

Some zen folk sit for hours every day for months. Some of them drop acid every other Sunday. Neither does an enlightened person make.
Exactly. And a friend I have who is further on the path than me put it an interesting way: dual and non-dual are just flavors. You get over the non-dual just like the dual.

That's kind of the trap of the non-dual revelation, honestly. Once you perceive non-duality, you return to the duality of duality vs non-duality. Every time you fold some aspect of nd vs. d back into the non-dual, each manifests as a new return to the duality of duality vs. non-duality.

Nirvana is that state when the awakening of non-duality reaches the extent that it transcends every possible manifestation of duality vs non-duality. Ala, gate gate paragate parasamgate, bodhi svaha. Keep going, keep going, keep going!

Zen is particularly self-aware of this, which is why I respect it. Most other traditions will only take you to initial awakening and then leave you floundering in the wind.

I live in a city on the lower side of a medium population (just under 200k), so we've got a few stores that sell comics and MTG cards but I was never sure if someone could just walk in and be like, "Hey, you don't know me and I've never done this before but will you take hours of your day and teach me". Tips on how to get into table top games?

No 1 person tabletop DND games, but plenty computer games. If you want to join a game, Check those stores websites for a calendar of events. When I got started, that's exactly what I did. I went in and said, I'd like to play Dungeons and Dragons. They said, every Wednesday 6pm. I started showing up.

That's what I've heard a bunch of people do... Quite honestly, how I got in was that I knew one guy who played it. I simply asked him, "hey, would you want to get a group together to play DnD over the summer?" and then we got a group of 6 together (5 players + DM) and we started playing every monday (when we got the time off). 4 of us had never played before; just the DM and the guy I talked to.

Look for any of the stores in your area that run D&D Adventures League.

That'll be pretty much exactly what you're looking for as a new player who doesn't have any buddies that are interested.

If you're up for playing online, then you can try Roll20. It's fantastic. They also have a Looking for Group (LFG) section you can find a group to play with. There are a lot of people willing to take on a new person.

Solendor mentioned the free download of D&D 5e Basic Rules, which is good, but I'd also suggest paying the $25 or whatever it is to get a Beginner Box. D&D 5e is, in my opinion, the more streamlined game, but the Pathfinder Beginner Box is superior in terms of quality and presentation. It's got a nice foldout map, sufficiently interesting introductory adventure (which will teach you the basics: fighting, various traps, searching, etc), and is definitely worth the money.

There are beginner boxes for lots of different games, such as the three for Star Wars. You could always buy a couple different genres, read through the introductory adventure and condensed rules books that come with them, and get a good idea of the different styles of games out there.

Also, just because they are Beginner Boxes doesn't mean they are really bare-bones. I actually ran a Pathfinder Beginner Box campaign for a long time. It only lacks some fiddly, more obscure rules. You can definitely play just with the content from the beginner box.
